CST201.start: If C syntax is new, skim the types and operators in Unit 1 before tracing the loops in Unit 2.

1.reason: These short expression traces and header explanations make a useful third pass. If syntax is the thing slowing you down, do this unit as a warm-up.
essentials: Group operators before evaluating an expression. Check integer division and casts separately.
Recognise basic types and tokens. Know what a header such as <stdio.h> declares.

reading.label: Operators in C
reading.cue: parenthesise a mixed expression and check precedence and associativity.

reading.label: Type conversion and casting
reading.cue: compare integer division with a division that has a floating-point operand.

1.try: Predict the results of 5/2 and 5/2.0, then trace one expression that mixes multiplication and addition. Explain where parentheses would change the result.

examples.task: Predict the result of an expression that mixes division, multiplication and addition.
Explain precedence, associativity and the difference between a header and a library.

quickReference.title: Group before evaluating
quickReference.rule: Precedence determines grouping. Associativity resolves ties at the same precedence level.
quickReference.example: 2 + 3 * 4 groups as 2 + (3 * 4) and gives 14. (2 + 3) * 4 gives 20.

quickReference.title: Division and casts
quickReference.rule: Integer division truncates toward zero. Convert an operand before dividing if you need a fractional result.
quickReference.example: 5 / 2 gives 2; (double)5 / 2 gives 2.5. Casting the result of 5 / 2 cannot restore the fraction.

quickReference.title: Bitwise AND
quickReference.rule: A result bit is 1 only when both corresponding input bits are 1.
quickReference.example: For 6 & 3: 0110 AND 0011 gives 0010, or 2.

patterns.title: Operator precedence and output tracing
patterns.prompt: Add parentheses to show how an expression is evaluated. Explain precedence and associativity, then predict the output of a short expression.

patterns.title: Header files and their purpose
patterns.prompt: Explain why a header is included, distinguish it from a library file, and name a relevant standard header in a short example.

patterns.title: Type conversion and integer division
patterns.prompt: Explain a cast or predict what happens to a value when the operands or the receiving type change. Check integer division separately.

patterns.title: Bitwise operators
patterns.prompt: Define bitwise operations and show one with a short bit pattern.

2.reason: Short loop templates cover written comparisons and full programs. The same dry run helps with both the running-total series and GCD.
essentials: Mark the test, body and update in a loop. Be able to explain why do–while runs its body at least once.
Trace a running total and a digit or GCD problem. Check one input that stops the loop early.

reading.label: Looping statements
reading.cue: compare where the test happens in while and do–while, then dry-run a for loop.

reading.label: Break and continue
reading.cue: explain which statements still run after each jump.

2.try: Trace digit sum with input 402, noting each remainder and updated value. Then write a GCD loop and test it with 18 and 12.

examples.task: Write the running-total series using loops.
Compare while and do–while, then write a GCD program.

quickReference.title: Before or after the body?
quickReference.rule: while tests first; do–while tests after its body.
quickReference.example: If x = 0 and the test is x > 0, while skips the body. A do–while with a body that leaves x unchanged runs once.

quickReference.title: Trace both totals
quickReference.rule: For a sum of running totals, update the inner total before adding it to the outer total.
quickReference.example: With i = 1, 2, 3, the inner totals are 1, 3, 6. Their total is 1 + 3 + 6 = 10.

quickReference.title: Euclid’s remainder step
quickReference.rule: Replace (a, b) with (b, a % b) while b is nonzero.

patterns.title: Compare loop types
patterns.prompt: Show when each loop tests its condition. Give an example where while and do–while behave differently.

patterns.title: Switch–case or nested if–else
patterns.prompt: Write a small branching program and explain when switch–case is a good fit. Be ready to draw the nested-if flow.

patterns.title: Sum a series of running totals
patterns.prompt: Given n, write a program to add 1, then 1 + 2, then 1 + 2 + 3, and so on. Trace your accumulator on a small input.

patterns.title: Explain loop control statements
patterns.prompt: Trace what break or continue changes, and explain why an unstructured jump can make the program harder to follow.

patterns.title: Find the GCD of two numbers
patterns.prompt: Write a loop for Euclid’s algorithm. Show how each remainder becomes the next divisor, and state when the loop stops.

3.reason: Matrix and string questions reuse loops you already know. A clear index trace is useful across several written question forms.
essentials: Write the row and column bounds before working on a matrix diagonal or transpose.
Leave room for the null terminator. Distinguish measuring, comparing and editing a string.

reading.label: Two-dimensional arrays
reading.cue: label rows and columns, then follow a diagonal or transpose example.

reading.label: Strings as character arrays
reading.cue: draw where the terminator goes before trying a string loop.

3.try: Sketch a 3 × 3 matrix, mark its diagonal indices, and write a loop that adds only those elements. Then draw how a short string is stored.

examples.task: Sum the diagonal of a 4 × 4 matrix.
Show string functions and check an input string for a palindrome.

quickReference.title: Main diagonal
quickReference.rule: For a square matrix, sum only positions whose row equals the column.

quickReference.title: Transpose
quickReference.rule: Move an element at row i, column j to row j, column i.
quickReference.example: A 2 × 3 matrix becomes a 3 × 2 matrix. The element a[0][2] goes to t[2][0].

quickReference.title: String storage
quickReference.rule: A C string ends at the first null character, written \0.
quickReference.example: char s[] = "cat" stores c, a, t, \0 in four slots; strlen(s) is 3.

patterns.title: Matrix programs
patterns.prompt: Write nested loops for a task such as finding diagonal elements, checking an identity matrix, or producing a transpose. Label rows and columns.

patterns.title: String library functions
patterns.prompt: Explain or implement the requested string operation: copy, concatenate, compare or find length. Give an input and the expected result.

patterns.title: Process a string character by character
patterns.prompt: Practise a manual string operation such as reversal, case conversion or a palindrome check. Show the indices you compare or advance.

patterns.title: Array declarations and subscripts
patterns.prompt: Declare a one-dimensional array, give an initializer and check which subscripts are valid. Explain why the last index is one less than the length.

4.reason: Storage-class comparisons and parameter examples are reusable. Recursion is worth practising after you can trace the same task with a loop.
essentials: Show which parameters receive copies and what the function returns. Use an address if the caller’s object must change.
Compare scope and lifetime, then trace a recursive base case and the return steps.

reading.label: Parameter passing
reading.cue: compare passing an integer with passing its address in a pointer parameter.

reading.label: Recursion
reading.cue: mark the stopping case and write the return values on the way back up.

4.try: Write a factorial function and trace the stack by hand for input 3. Test the base case separately.

examples.task: Compare storage classes and passing a value versus an address.
Write a recursive factorial function.

quickReference.title: Value versus address
quickReference.rule: C passes arguments by value. A copied pointer still points to the caller’s object.
quickReference.example: If a function takes int *p and executes *p = 9 after being called with &x, the caller’s x becomes 9.

quickReference.title: Scope and lifetime
quickReference.rule: Scope is where a name is visible; lifetime is how long the object exists.
quickReference.example: A local static counter initialised to 0 and incremented on each call retains its value between calls.

quickReference.title: Recursive returns
quickReference.rule: Specify a base case, then reduce each call toward it.
quickReference.example: With fact(0) = 1, fact(3) is 3 × fact(2), which unwinds to 3 × 2 × 1 × 1 = 6.

patterns.title: Storage classes and scope
patterns.prompt: Explain the common storage classes with small declarations. Compare scope, lifetime and the behaviour of repeated calls.

patterns.title: Passing arguments by value or address
patterns.prompt: Use one small example to show why passing a value does not change the caller’s variable but using its address can.

patterns.title: Function declaration and parameters
patterns.prompt: Distinguish a prototype or declaration from a definition. Label actual and formal parameters in an example call.

patterns.title: Recursive functions
patterns.prompt: Write a base case and show the call sequence for a numeric example. Be able to compare the recursive and iterative versions.

5.firstPractice: Draw what a pointer refers to
5.reason: Pointers turn up in written questions, but correct traversal and allocation take more careful tracing. Start them after arrays and function calls.
essentials: Draw the pointer, the address and the object separately. Check the array bound before dereferencing.
For dynamic memory, calculate the size, check allocation, use the block and free it once.

reading.label: Declaring and accessing pointers
reading.cue: explain what & and * mean in a short example.

reading.label: Dynamic memory allocation
reading.cue: compare malloc, calloc and realloc, then mark where free belongs.

5.try: Draw a small dynamically allocated array. Write the allocation, failure check, traversal and cleanup in that order.

examples.task: Explain address-of and dereference, then access an array using pointers.
Explain malloc, calloc, realloc and free.

quickReference.title: Address and dereference
quickReference.rule: For an object x, &x is its address; *p accesses the object that p points to.
quickReference.example: Declare int x = 4 and int *p = &x. Assigning *p = 7 changes x to 7.

quickReference.title: Array access
quickReference.rule: Within the array, a[i] accesses the same element as *(a + i).
quickReference.example: For a = {5, 8, 13}, *(a + 1) reads 8. Index 3 is outside the three elements.

quickReference.title: Allocate, then check
quickReference.rule: Size a block by the element count times the size of one element. Check before use; free it when finished.
quickReference.example: For three int values, allocate 3 * sizeof *p bytes for an int pointer p. Do not dereference a null result.

patterns.title: Pointer declarations and dereferencing
patterns.prompt: Show a valid declaration and label the address-of and dereference operations. Explain what the pointer refers to.

patterns.title: Array access with pointers
patterns.prompt: Traverse an array or find an element through a pointer. Relate pointer arithmetic to the element type and the array indices.

patterns.title: Dynamic allocation routines
patterns.prompt: Compare malloc, calloc, realloc and free. In a program, show where allocation is checked and where memory is released.

patterns.title: Pointer to a function
patterns.prompt: Explain what a pointer to a function refers to, and sketch a declaration and a call using it.

checklist: Trace one loop on a normal input and a boundary case.
Explain the index bounds of a matrix and the terminator of a C string.
Identify the return value and base case of a recursive function.
Draw what a pointer refers to and say where allocated memory is freed.

CST203.topics: Python basics, functions, files and Django
CST203.start: Predict the output before running a snippet. Use Unit 1 as a warm-up if types or slices slow you down.

1.reason: Comparing collections and dry-running slices are short tasks with both objective and written examples in the archive.
essentials: Choose among a mutable list, an immutable tuple and a dictionary keyed by a lookup value.
Trace indexing and slicing. Explain what split and join return on the same short string.

reading.label: Lists, tuples and dictionaries
reading.cue: make a tiny example of each and try changing one value.

reading.label: Strings and slicing
reading.cue: check the excluded stop index and practise split and join.

1.try: Make a list of five values. Predict two slices and try changing an element; explain how the same operation differs on a tuple.

examples.task: Compare lists, tuples and dictionaries, and distinguish indexing from slicing.
Show what join and split do and explain string immutability.

quickReference.title: Index versus slice
quickReference.rule: An index picks one element; a slice normally excludes its stop index.

quickReference.title: Choose a collection
quickReference.rule: Use a list for a mutable sequence, a tuple for a fixed sequence, or a dict for key lookup.
quickReference.example: scores = {"Mina": 7} lets you look up scores["Mina"] directly instead of remembering a list position.

quickReference.title: Split and join
quickReference.rule: split produces pieces; separator.join puts string pieces together.
quickReference.example: "a,b,c".split(",") gives ["a", "b", "c"]. "-".join of those pieces gives "a-b-c".

patterns.title: Lists, tuples and dictionaries
patterns.prompt: Compare how lists, tuples and dictionaries store and change values. Give a short example and identify which examples are mutable.

patterns.title: Indexing and slicing
patterns.prompt: Predict which elements a slice selects. Explain the difference between a slice and an index using a small list.

patterns.title: String methods and formatting
patterns.prompt: Show what split and join return. Practise a string-formatting example and explain why changing one character does not mutate a string.

patterns.title: Data types and conversions
patterns.prompt: Identify built-in types in examples and show how to convert a number or string. Explain when the interpreter converts a value and when an explicit conversion is needed.

patterns.title: Membership, identity and other operators
patterns.prompt: Demonstrate an operator with a short expression and explain the result. In particular, distinguish membership, equality and identity.

2.reason: Loop traces and small programs appear repeatedly. One dry-run habit transfers to range, prime checks and break/continue questions.
essentials: Trace if/elif/else, indentation and range bounds. Test the first, last and empty cases.
Explain break, continue and pass by showing which line executes next.

reading.label: Loops and range
reading.cue: write down each value produced by range before tracing the body.

reading.label: Loop control statements
reading.cue: compare exit, skip-to-next-iteration and no operation.

2.try: Write a prime checker and dry-run it on 1, 2 and 9. Mark exactly which condition rejects a composite number.

examples.task: Explain break, continue and pass, then write a prime checker.
Compare for and while and write a digit-sum program.

quickReference.title: End of a range
quickReference.rule: The stop value is excluded.
quickReference.example: range(2, 6, 2) yields 2 and 4, not 6.

quickReference.title: Three loop controls
quickReference.rule: break exits the innermost loop, continue skips the rest of this iteration, and pass does nothing.
quickReference.example: Over [1, 2, 3], skipping 2 with continue leaves 1 and 3 to print. Breaking at 2 prints only 1.

quickReference.title: Prime check
quickReference.rule: Reject values below 2, then look for a divisor up to and including the square root.
quickReference.example: For 9 the divisor 3 makes the remainder zero. For 2 there is no candidate divisor to test.

patterns.title: Trace loops and range
patterns.prompt: Compare for and while, then predict the values a small range-based loop prints. Identify the update and the stopping condition.

patterns.title: Break, continue and pass
patterns.prompt: On the same loop input, show which iteration is skipped or which statement ends the loop. Distinguish pass from both.

patterns.title: Check whether a value is a palindrome
patterns.prompt: Write a short program for the numeric or string version in the paper. Check a palindrome, a non-palindrome and a one-character case.

patterns.title: Test whether a number is prime
patterns.prompt: Write a divisibility loop. Test it with 1, 2 and a composite number, and explain when the loop can stop.

patterns.title: Indentation and conditional branching
patterns.prompt: Mark the statements inside and outside an indented branch, then show which branch runs on two inputs.

3.reason: Function-argument and scope questions reuse a few compact examples. Practise those before writing longer scripts or following imports.
essentials: Explain positional, keyword, default and variable-length arguments with calls to a small function.
Distinguish a local name from a module-level name, and a module from a package.

reading.label: Parameters and arguments
reading.cue: compare a call that supplies a value with one that uses the default.

reading.label: Modules and imports
reading.cue: trace where an imported function is defined and how it is called.

3.try: Write a function with one default argument, call it with and without that argument, and move it to a module that you import.

examples.task: Give examples of positional, default and variable-length arguments.
Compare module and package, and distinguish local, global and nonlocal scope.

quickReference.title: Default argument
quickReference.rule: A parameter’s default is used when the caller leaves that argument out.
quickReference.example: For def scale(n, k=2): return n*k, scale(3) returns 6 and scale(3, k=4) returns 12.

quickReference.title: Local versus global
quickReference.rule: An ordinary assignment inside a function binds a local name unless declared otherwise.
quickReference.example: With x = 10 at module level, a function that assigns x = 3 and returns x yields 3 without changing the module’s x.

quickReference.title: Module import
quickReference.rule: A module supplies named objects. A package can group related modules.
quickReference.example: If tools.py defines double, import tools makes tools.double(3) available when tools.py is on the import path.

patterns.title: Function arguments and return
patterns.prompt: Demonstrate positional, default, keyword or variable-length arguments. Use a small call and state what is returned.

patterns.title: Scope of variables
patterns.prompt: Show which names are available inside and outside a function. Distinguish local, global and nonlocal scope using an example.

patterns.title: Modules, packages and imports
patterns.prompt: Compare a module with a package, draw a tiny package layout and give a valid import statement.

patterns.title: Lambda functions
patterns.prompt: Explain a lambda with a one-expression example. State its inputs and result, and compare with an ordinary named function.

4.firstPractice: Pick a file mode and match
4.reason: File questions are useful, but modes, read/write methods and regex returns need separate practice. Learn them after the short reusable answers.
essentials: Choose between read, overwrite and append. Know what read, readline and readlines return.
Compare re.match, re.search and re.findall using input where the first match is not at the start.

reading.label: File I/O operations
reading.cue: read the mode table and a with-block before trying read or write.

reading.label: Regular expressions
reading.cue: trace which API returns one match and which returns a list.

4.try: Read a short text file, count its lines, and use a regular expression to pick out digit groups from the text.

examples.task: Explain file access modes and show read and write methods.
Compare re.match, re.split and re.findall with examples.

quickReference.title: Read, write, or append
quickReference.rule: r reads an existing file, w creates or truncates, and a creates or appends.
quickReference.example: To add a new line to a log without discarding earlier lines, choose a rather than w.

quickReference.title: One line at a time
quickReference.rule: readline returns the next line, while readlines returns a list of the remaining lines.
quickReference.example:
For a file containing A
B
, the first readline gives "A
"; a subsequent readlines gives ["B
"].

quickReference.title: Regex starting position
quickReference.rule: match checks the start of a string, search looks anywhere, and findall can collect all matching spans.
quickReference.example: On "A12 B3", re.match(r"\d+", text) returns None; re.findall with that pattern returns ["12", "3"].

patterns.title: Choose a file mode
patterns.prompt: Explain what happens when opening an existing or missing file in the requested mode. Use a separate example for reading, writing and appending.

patterns.title: Read and write methods
patterns.prompt: Compare the file methods by the data they return or accept. Demonstrate read, readline, readlines, write and writelines where relevant.

patterns.title: Work with a text file
patterns.prompt: Practise an open–read–process–close solution. For a word count, explain how the text is split and counted; for output, state what is written.

patterns.title: Regular-expression matching
patterns.prompt: Explain pattern matching and compare methods such as match, split and findall on one short test string.

5.reason: Start with the repeatable architecture diagram and template purpose. Project setup and forms can follow as separate practice.
essentials: Trace a request through the URL pattern and view to the response. Explain the role of the model and template.
Distinguish template data from static assets. Practise one template tag for a CSS file.

reading.label: MVC and Django’s roles
reading.cue: label which part stores data, which renders it and which handles the request.

reading.label: URLs and templates
reading.cue: follow a request to the view, then show where template context is used.

5.try: Draw the route for a page that lists books, labelling what receives the URL and what displays the list. Add where a form would be validated.

examples.task: Describe Django’s MVC/MTV architecture.
Show how to insert a static file into a Django template.

quickReference.title: Request flow
quickReference.rule: A URL pattern selects a view. The view returns the response and can render a template.
quickReference.example: For /books/, a books view could load a book list and render books.html with that list in the context.

quickReference.title: Model, template and view
quickReference.rule: A model describes the data, a template presents it, and a view coordinates the request.
quickReference.example: A Book model stores titles. The view supplies the books; the template loops through them to show the titles.

quickReference.title: Static assets
quickReference.rule: Static CSS and images are files; template context is per-request data.
quickReference.example: After {% load static %}, use {% static "css/main.css" %} to build the asset URL in a template.

patterns.title: Explain MVC and Django’s MTV architecture
patterns.prompt: Label the responsibilities in a diagram. Describe how the model, template and view work together for a page request.

patterns.title: Templates and static assets
patterns.prompt: Explain why a template is used for page output and how static files can be referenced or managed.

patterns.title: What Django is and when to use it
patterns.prompt: Describe why a web app might use Django. When comparing with Flask, state your project assumptions instead of claiming one is always better.

patterns.title: Create and run a Django project
patterns.prompt: Outline the setup and run steps. Practise explaining the difference between a project and an app as you walk through the process.

checklist: Predict a slice and the output of a loop before you run either.
Show a call with a default argument and explain what the function returns.
Pick a file mode and a regular-expression method for a small task.
Sketch a Django URL, view and template flow without looking at the notes.

CST205.topics: Stacks, queues, linked lists, trees and graphs
CST205.start: Draw every index or link that changes. If the names of the structures are unfamiliar, skim Unit 1 first.

1.reason: The definitions are fast to revise, but most of the practice here is comparing and explaining. Put the reusable stack and linked-list algorithms first unless the terms are unfamiliar.
essentials: Give one linear and one non-linear example and explain how their elements are organised.
Describe an ADT by its behaviour before naming an implementation. Know traversal, insertion and deletion.

reading.label: Classification of data structures
reading.cue: compare a linear sequence with a branching structure.

reading.label: Abstract data types
reading.cue: list the permitted operations without choosing an array or links yet.

1.try: Pick a linear structure and a non-linear one. Sketch both and describe what it means to visit every element in each.

examples.task: Define a data structure and compare linear with non-linear structures.
Give an example of an abstract data type.

quickReference.title: Linear or non-linear?
quickReference.rule: A linear structure organises elements in a sequence; a tree branches.
quickReference.example: A queue of A, B, C has a single order. A root with two children illustrates a non-linear structure.

quickReference.title: ADT and implementation
quickReference.rule: An ADT describes operations and behaviour, not the memory representation.
quickReference.example: A stack promises LIFO removal. An array or linked list can implement the same push and pop behaviour.

quickReference.title: Delete from an array
quickReference.rule: With a packed array, deleting an element leaves a gap that later elements must fill.
quickReference.example: Delete index 1 from [4, 7, 9]: shift 9 left and reduce the logical length to get [4, 9].

patterns.title: Linear and non-linear structures
patterns.prompt: Classify examples by how their elements relate. Give a clear difference with a linear and a non-linear example.

patterns.title: Primitive types and structures
patterns.prompt: Define primitive and non-primitive structures and distinguish a data type from a data structure using an example.

patterns.title: Abstract data type
patterns.prompt: Define an ADT and give an example. Describe its operations before choosing how to implement them.

patterns.title: Common operations and their preconditions
patterns.prompt: Explain insertion, deletion and traversal. Discuss what happens if insertion is attempted without spare capacity.

2.reason: Push/pop, postfix and circular queues recur in full questions. One trace table helps with algorithms, boundary cases and objective items.
essentials: Trace the top index for push/pop and cover overflow and underflow. Use the stack state to check each postfix token.
Mark front and rear after each circular queue operation, including wraparound.

reading.label: Stack operations
reading.cue: check the empty and full conditions before changing top.

reading.label: Queue types
reading.cue: focus on the circular queue and draw its wraparound.

2.try: Evaluate the postfix expression 8 3 − 2 × with a stack. Then use a circular capacity of four and trace rear as it wraps after a dequeue.

examples.task: Write push and pop algorithms with overflow and underflow checks.
Write circular-queue insertion and deletion algorithms.

quickReference.title: Stack top
quickReference.rule: A stack removes the most recently pushed item. In a zero-based array implementation, top = −1 denotes empty.
quickReference.example: Push 4, then 9: top changes −1 → 0 → 1. Pop returns 9 and leaves top at 0.

quickReference.title: Postfix subtraction
quickReference.rule: When applying a binary operator, the first popped value is the right operand.
quickReference.example: For 9 2 − 3 ×, pop 2 then 9 for 9 − 2 = 7. Multiply by 3 to get 21.

quickReference.title: Circular queue wrap
quickReference.rule: When space exists, an index advances to (index + 1) mod capacity.
quickReference.example: In four slots, rear = 3 advances to 0 on the next insertion if slot 0 is free.

patterns.title: Stack push, pop and boundary cases
patterns.prompt: Write the array-based push and pop algorithms. Trace the top index, including full and empty cases.

patterns.title: Infix and postfix exercises
patterns.prompt: Use a stack to convert or evaluate the expression requested in the paper. Record the stack state after each token.

patterns.title: Circular queue operations
patterns.prompt: Trace insertion and deletion with a front and rear. Show when each index wraps and explain how full and empty are distinguished.

patterns.title: Deque and restricted operations
patterns.prompt: Draw the two ends of a deque and distinguish input-restricted from output-restricted operations.

patterns.title: Recursive problem solving
patterns.prompt: Identify the base case and show smaller calls in a GCD or Tower of Hanoi solution. Compare recursion with iteration.

3.reason: Insertion and comparison questions reuse a before/after diagram. Practise singly linked lists first, then add back links or a circular tail.
essentials: Draw the head, changed link and next node for inserts and deletes. Include the empty-list case.
Compare a null-terminated list with a circular list, and show which back links a doubly linked list needs.

reading.label: Singly linked-list insertion
reading.cue: trace head, middle and tail cases before writing the code.

reading.label: Four list types
reading.cue: compare the stopping condition and the links stored per node.

3.try: On paper, insert into an empty list, insert in the middle, and delete the last node. Label which references change each time.

examples.task: Insert a node at the beginning of a singly linked list.
Compare a linked list with an array and describe the advantage of back links.

quickReference.title: Insert after a node
quickReference.rule: Preserve the old successor before replacing the predecessor’s link.
quickReference.example: For A → B, set X.next = B and A.next = X to get A → X → B.

quickReference.title: Doubly linked pair
quickReference.rule: An adjacent pair needs a forward link and a matching backward link.
quickReference.example: Inserting X between A and B sets A.next = X, X.prev = A, X.next = B and B.prev = X.

quickReference.title: Circular stop condition
quickReference.rule: In a nonempty circular list the tail links back to the head, not to NULL.
quickReference.example: With A → B → A and head A, visit A and B once; stop when the next pointer returns to A.

patterns.title: Insert into a singly linked list
patterns.prompt: Write an insertion algorithm and sketch the affected links. Trace the separate cases for the beginning, middle and end of the list.

patterns.title: Array versus linked list
patterns.prompt: Compare storage and access, then give a case where you would choose each representation.

patterns.title: Doubly linked-list behaviour
patterns.prompt: Label previous and next links, explain the benefit of two-way traversal and show which references are updated.

patterns.title: Circular linked lists
patterns.prompt: Draw a circular linked list, explain the last link and distinguish it from a list that terminates with NULL.

patterns.title: Represent a polynomial as a linked list
patterns.prompt: Draw a node layout for a polynomial term and show how links connect the terms of the given expression.

4.reason: Trees and graph traversals have good past-paper coverage, but they need several distinct traces. Give AVL, traversal and graph work separate time.
essentials: Write pre-, in- and post-order on one tree. Reconstruct a tree with distinct keys and practise an AVL rotation separately.
Run BFS and DFS from a named start with a fixed neighbour order, marking visited vertices.

reading.label: Tree traversals
reading.cue: write the position of the root in each visit order.

reading.label: BFS and DFS
reading.cue: trace the queue or stack and mark when each vertex is first visited.

4.try: Take a small tree and write all three traversal orders. On a small graph, run BFS and DFS from the same vertex and compare the orders.

examples.task: Reconstruct the tree from in-order and pre-order and give post-order.
Explain AVL rotations and construct an AVL tree from the given values.

quickReference.title: Reconstruct from two orders
quickReference.rule: With distinct keys, pre-order gives the root first; in-order separates its left and right subtrees.
quickReference.example: Pre-order B, A, C and in-order A, B, C give B at the root. Post-order is A, C, B.

quickReference.title: AVL rotation
quickReference.rule: Identify the first unbalanced node on the insertion path and the side of the imbalance.
quickReference.example: Inserting 30, 20, 10 creates an LL case. Rotate right at 30 to make 20 the root.

quickReference.title: Compare BFS and DFS
quickReference.rule: BFS uses a queue; DFS goes deep first using recursion or a stack.
quickReference.example: On edges A–B, A–C, B–D from A with alphabetical neighbours, BFS is A, B, C, D; DFS is A, B, D, C.

patterns.title: Tree traversals and reconstruction
patterns.prompt: Use the given in-order and pre-order lists to reconstruct the tree. Check the result by producing another traversal.

patterns.title: AVL trees and rotations

patterns.title: B-tree properties and construction

1.reason: A labelled computer diagram and a short register trace are easy to rehearse. Do the floating-point exercises as a second pass within this unit.
essentials: Label the CPU, memory and I/O, plus the address, data and control paths.

examples.task: Draw the Von Neumann blocks and explain the buses.
Compare fixed-point and floating-point formats, then encode −75 in eight bits.

quickReference.title: Three buses
quickReference.rule: The address identifies a location, the data bus carries the value, and control coordinates the operation.
quickReference.example: On a CPU memory read, the CPU supplies an address and a read signal; memory supplies the data.

quickReference.title: Eight-bit negative value
quickReference.rule: For two’s complement, invert the fixed-width positive bits and add 1.
quickReference.example: +6 is 00000110. Inverting and adding 1 gives 11111010 for −6 in eight bits.

quickReference.title: Binary32 normal numbers
quickReference.rule: Normal IEEE binary32 values use one sign bit, eight exponent bits with bias 127, and 23 fraction bits.
quickReference.example: 1.5 = 1.1₂ × 2⁰: sign 0, exponent field 127, and fraction starting with 1 then zeros.

patterns.title: Von Neumann architecture and buses
patterns.prompt: Draw a labelled computer diagram and show how instructions and data reach the CPU. Explain what each bus carries.

patterns.title: Floating-point representation
patterns.prompt: Label the sign, exponent and fraction fields of an IEEE representation. When asked, compare fixed-point and floating-point formats.

patterns.title: Two’s complement representation
patterns.prompt: Write the requested negative number using the stated bit width, and show the intermediate steps.

patterns.title: Register micro-operations and shifts
patterns.prompt: Identify a register micro-operation and trace a shift on a small register value. State which bits enter and leave the register.

2.reason: This unit has substantial written examples, but arithmetic traces, control sequencing and hazards are separate skills. Tackle them once the shorter diagrams are secure.
essentials: Draw overlapping instruction stages and distinguish structural, data and control hazards.
Keep control memory and arithmetic traces separate. For Booth and restoring division, label the registers after each step.

reading.cue: mark one dependency on a stage timeline and show why a stall can occur.

reading.label: Computer arithmetic
reading.cue: practise a Booth decision and a restoring-division iteration separately.

2.try: Trace a small signed multiplication using the taught register format. Draw a separate pipeline timeline and mark where a dependency can delay an instruction.

examples.task: Explain pipelining and identify the kinds of hazards.
Multiply two negative numbers using Booth’s algorithm.

quickReference.title: Overlapping stages
quickReference.rule: Pipelining overlaps work on different instructions; throughput and single-instruction latency are different.
quickReference.example: Without a stall, instruction 1 can decode in cycle 2 while instruction 2 fetches in cycle 2.

quickReference.title: One Booth decision
quickReference.rule: For the pair (Q₀, Q₋₁), 01 adds M and 10 subtracts M from A before the arithmetic shift.
quickReference.example: If the pair is 10, A = 0000 and M = 0011, subtract to get A = 1101 in four bits before shifting.

quickReference.title: Microprogrammed control
quickReference.rule: A microinstruction selects control actions and how to obtain the next microinstruction.
quickReference.example: A fetch sequence can include MAR ← PC, followed by requesting a memory read and receiving the instruction.

patterns.title: Pipelining and hazards
patterns.prompt: Draw the stages and identify a hazard on a short timeline. Explain how a mitigation changes the execution.

patterns.title: Microprogrammed control
patterns.prompt: Draw the control-memory path and explain address sequencing. Compare with hardwired control when the paper asks for it.

patterns.title: Signed multiplication with Booth’s algorithm

patterns.title: Restoring division

patterns.title: Vector processing
patterns.prompt: Explain what a vector instruction does to a collection of elements. Give one example and distinguish it from a scalar operation.

3.reason: Addressing-mode questions recur and the architecture uses repeatable diagrams. Rehearse one example per mode before studying all pin details.

quickReference.title: BIU and EU
quickReference.rule: The BIU handles bus transfers and instruction fetch. The EU decodes and executes instructions.
quickReference.example: The BIU fills the instruction queue; the EU consumes instruction bytes from that queue.

quickReference.title: Segment and offset
quickReference.rule: Form an 8086 physical address from the segment value times 16 plus the offset.

quickReference.title: Immediate or memory?
quickReference.rule: An immediate value is encoded in the instruction; register-indirect addressing gets a memory offset from a register.
quickReference.example: MOV AX, 0005h loads the value 5. MOV AX, [BX] reads a word from memory using BX as the offset.

4.reason: A short register trace is a good first drill, but the archived examples here are less consistent than those for 8086 addressing or cache. Use the notes for branches, procedures and macros as well.
essentials: Keep the destination and source straight. Record the registers a move or arithmetic instruction changes.
Explain the difference between a jump, a procedure call and a stack-machine expression. Do not mix their notation.

reading.cue: trace a short add-and-store example register by register.

examples.task: Choose an assembly sequence that adds two registers and saves the result.
Write zero-address instructions to evaluate an arithmetic expression.

quickReference.title: Read destination first
quickReference.rule: In 8086 Intel syntax, MOV destination, source copies the value without changing the source.
quickReference.example: With AX = 2 and BX = 3, ADD AX, BX gives AX = 5; MOV CX, AX then gives CX = 5.

quickReference.title: Call or jump?
quickReference.rule: CALL saves a return address; an ordinary JMP does not.
quickReference.example: If CALL transfers to a procedure, RET can resume at the instruction following the CALL.

quickReference.title: Zero-address expression
quickReference.rule: On an abstract stack machine, an operator takes operands from the stack, not explicit register arguments.
quickReference.example: To evaluate 8 − 3, push 8, push 3, then subtract the top from the next item. The result on the stack is 5.

patterns.title: Data movement instructions

patterns.title: Register arithmetic and result storage

patterns.title: Stack-based instructions for expressions

patterns.title: Calls and interrupts

patterns.title: Input/output instructions

5.reason: Mapping comparisons and hit-ratio questions reuse similar worked examples. Add memory interfacing after you can distinguish cache and address translation.
essentials: Compare cache mappings and state what a miss time includes before calculating average access time.

quickReference.title: Direct mapping
quickReference.rule: With L lines, block b maps to line b mod L. The tag determines whether the desired block is present.
quickReference.example: With eight lines, block 14 maps to line 6. Check the tag before calling it a hit.

quickReference.title: Average access time
quickReference.rule: Weight the total time for a hit and for a miss by their probabilities.
quickReference.example: With 90% hits at 2 ns and a total miss time of 22 ns: 0.9 × 2 + 0.1 × 22 = 4 ns.

quickReference.title: Page and offset
quickReference.rule: Translation replaces the page number with a frame number while keeping the offset.
quickReference.example: With 4 KiB pages, virtual 0x1234 has page 1 and offset 0x234. If page 1 maps to frame 7, the address is 0x7234.

patterns.prompt: Compare direct, associative and set-associative mapping. Use a small address example to explain a direct-mapped cache.

patterns.prompt: Explain virtual memory and the TLB. Where asked, distinguish virtual addresses from physical memory or cache mapping.

1.reason: The definitions are quick, but search and sort traces give you more chances to practise a complete procedure. If you get stuck on the notation, use this unit as a warm-up.
essentials: State what the algorithm receives and produces. Distinguish time from extra space.

Count iterations in a loop whose index doubles.

quickReference.title: Growth bounds
quickReference.rule: O is an upper bound; Ω is a lower bound; Θ is a tight bound.
quickReference.example: Example: 3n + 4 grows as Θ(n).

quickReference.title: Count a loop
quickReference.rule: Write out the values before naming the time bound.
quickReference.example: Starting at 1 and doubling while i ≤ 16 gives 1, 2, 4, 8, 16: five iterations.

quickReference.title: Divide and conquer
quickReference.rule: Split the input, solve the subproblems, then combine the results.
quickReference.example: Merge sort splits in half and merges in linear time: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n).

quickReference.title: One pass
quickReference.rule: Bubble compares adjacent items; selection picks the smallest remaining item.
quickReference.example: On [4, 3, 2, 1], the first ascending bubble pass gives [3, 2, 1, 4]. The first selection pass gives [1, 3, 2, 4].

quickReference.title: Worst-case costs
quickReference.rule: Selection and insertion take Θ(n²); merge sort and heapsort take Θ(n log n).
quickReference.example: Quicksort can take Θ(n²) when each pivot leaves one partition almost as large as the input.

quickReference.title: Radix sort by digits
quickReference.rule: Least-significant-digit radix sort needs a stable sort at each digit.

quickReference.title: Binary search
quickReference.rule: Check the midpoint of the sorted interval and keep only the possible half.
quickReference.example: To find 8 in [2, 4, 6, 8, 10], check 6, keep [8, 10], then check 8 (rounding the midpoint down).

quickReference.title: Hash collision
quickReference.rule: 7 mod 5 = 12 mod 5 = 2.
quickReference.example: Chaining stores both keys in bucket 2. Probing looks for another slot instead.

quickReference.title: Search costs
quickReference.rule: Worst-case time on arrays: linear O(n), binary O(log n).
quickReference.example: Binary search needs sorted input; linear search can scan an unsorted array.

4.reason: Graph questions provide written practice, but shortest paths, minimum spanning trees and topological order solve different problems. Keep a separate trace for each.

quickReference.title: Two different goals
quickReference.rule: An MST minimizes total tree weight. A shortest path minimizes cost between vertices.
quickReference.example: In an undirected triangle with A–B = 2, B–C = 3, A–C = 4, the MST costs 5. The shortest A-to-C path is the direct edge of weight 4.

quickReference.title: Relax an edge
quickReference.rule: Replace d[v] if d[u] + w(u,v) is smaller. Dijkstra needs non-negative edge weights.
quickReference.example: If d[u] = 3, w(u,v) = 2 and d[v] = 8, update d[v] to 5.

quickReference.title: All-pairs shortest paths
quickReference.rule: Floyd–Warshall tests each vertex k as an intermediate stop.
quickReference.example: If i→k costs 2 and k→j costs 4, a current i→j distance of 9 drops to 6.

quickReference.title: Topological order
quickReference.rule: Only a DAG has a topological order. Every edge points from an earlier vertex to a later one.
quickReference.example: If A→C and B→C, put both A and B before C.
